title: How can a wallet sign messages for different address types?
dek: A message signature shows that someone could satisfy an address’s spending conditions for that message. It does not establish their identity or a lasting balance.

blocks.text: Legacy Bitcoin message signing was specified only for P2PKH addresses. It could not express the spending conditions of other address types. BIP 322 uses Bitcoin Script itself, so message signing can cover SegWit, Taproot and multisignature scripts as well.

Someone asks you to prove you can use a Bitcoin address. Sending a payment would demonstrate a spend, but it would also move coins. BIP 322 instead builds a pair of virtual transactions around a message and asks for the data that would satisfy the address’s script.

The result belongs to that message and that address. It is evidence that someone could satisfy the script before presenting it. It does not tell the verifier who that person is, whether they sent an earlier payment, or whether they still control any coins.

figure.title: What the signature proves
figure.caption: The message and address define the challenge. A valid response satisfies that script; identity, freshness and a current balance need separate evidence.

sections.heading: Make the message say what you need

blocks.text: A signature carries no reliable creation date. Its lock-time field T is a spending condition, not a timestamp. Freshness has to come from the message—for example, a challenge chosen by the verifier. Even a fresh response cannot promise that coins will remain unspent afterward.

The authors also caution that someone may sign messages on another person’s behalf while refusing to sign a real transaction for them. A message signature cannot settle every question of ownership or control.

Because to_sign looks like a transaction, signing devices need care. When a signer recognises a BIP 322 request it must show the user the message and the address, and the BIP asks that the screens resemble signing a message, not spending 0 satoshis.

blocks.summary: What a proof of funds can establish

blocks.text: What BIP 322 sets out to show, in its authors’ words, is narrower: that the signer will be able to control funds sent to the address. It cannot show that the signer sent some earlier transaction. A proof of funds can list UTXOs, but it does not show they are all the address holds, nor that they are still unspent; a verifier needs the current UTXO set for that.

sections.heading: A spend that cannot move coins

blocks.text: The first virtual transaction, to_spend, pays to the address’s script and commits to the message. Its input names an output that does not exist. The second, to_sign, spends that virtual output. Satisfying its input script produces the message signature.

blocks.title: to_spend and to_sign
blocks.caption: Six of BIP 322’s published vectors. The address and message determine to_spend; the response supplies what to_sign needs to spend it. The wrong-message example fails verification.

blocks.text: Neither transaction is meant to be broadcast. The nonexistent input prevents to_spend from being relayed as an ordinary transaction, and to_sign depends on it. The authors chose this shape so existing transaction-signing hardware could support message signing.

The message hash is a BIP 340 tagged hash with the tag BIP0322-signed-message, taken over the message exactly as given, with no length prefix and no terminator. Change the message, even by one character, and the hash changes, and so does to_spend’s ID.

blocks.title: Another message, another hash
blocks.caption: Two of BIP 322’s vectors for the same address with different messages: unrelated hashes, so different to_spend transactions.

blocks.text: Except for the deliberately missing coin, the pair must satisfy the consensus rules. A script may require more than one signature, or no cryptographic signature at all. The published 3-of-3 multisig example contains three ECDSA signatures, an empty dummy item and the witness script.

blocks.title: A signature that is a witness stack
blocks.caption: The 3-of-3 multisig vector’s signature, item by item: an empty dummy, three ECDSA signatures and the witness script.

blocks.summary: The fields of the two virtual transactions

blocks.text: The construction uses two virtual transactions. The first, to_spend, commits to the message and the address. Its single input spends output 0xFFFFFFFF of a transaction whose ID is all zeros, an output that does not exist, and its scriptSig pushes the message hash. Its single output pays 0 satoshis to the address’s script, which the BIP calls the message challenge.

The second, to_sign, spends to_spend’s output 0 and pays 0 satoshis to a bare OP_RETURN. The signer fills in its witness, or in the full format its scriptSig and other fields too, exactly as they would to spend a real coin locked to the address. In the simple format that witness is the signature; in the full format, the whole signed to_sign is.

sections.heading: How much of the proof is sent?

blocks.text: The simple format sends only the witness. The verifier can rebuild everything else when the address is native SegWit and the virtual transaction uses its defaults. The full format sends the signed transaction too, which allows scriptSigs and time locks. Proof of funds adds inputs naming the UTXOs to demonstrate and carries the result in a finalized PSBT.

blocks.title: Three ways to carry the response
blocks.caption: The format determines what the verifier receives and what it reconstructs. The older legacy format remains restricted to P2PKH.

blocks.text: The simple format, prefixed smp, carries only the witness stack. It may be used only when to_sign keeps all its defaults, nothing added and version, sequence and lock time left at 0, and the address is native SegWit: P2WPKH, P2WSH or P2TR. The verifier rebuilds both transactions itself.

The full format, prefixed ful, carries the whole signed to_sign transaction. It covers every script type, including P2PKH and P2SH, which need a scriptSig, and scripts with time locks, which need to_sign’s version, lock time or sequence set. The proof-of-funds variant, prefixed pof, adds further inputs for any UTXOs the signer wants to show control of, and travels as a finalized PSBT.

Signers MUST put the prefix on. A verifier may still read an unprefixed signature as simple, for compatibility with implementations written before the BIP was finalized; one of the published vectors tests exactly that. The legacy format MAY still be used, but MUST be restricted to P2PKH addresses, and new proofs SHOULD use the new formats for every address type, P2PKH included.

Signing for a multisig address works the way spending from one does. Each signer produces a partial signature on to_sign, coordinated through a PSBT, and BIP 322 adds one global PSBT field, number 0x09, that carries the message itself. The BIP recommends keeping messages to a few kilobytes and committing to very large ones by hash.

blocks.summary: Legacy signatures and the proposal’s history

blocks.text: Exchanges, auditors and counterparties sometimes ask: can you show that this address is yours? The old answer, the legacy signmessage format, was specified only for P2PKH addresses, the ones starting with 1, as the BIP’s authors note. Its signatures also have a flaw the BIP’s authors spell out: they are ECDSA signatures that do not commit to the public key, so they do not actually prove knowledge of a secret key, and third parties can tweak a valid one into a valid signature for certain related keys.

BIP 322, assigned in 2018 and recorded as Complete at version 2.0.0, replaces the special-purpose signature with Bitcoin Script itself. A message signature becomes whatever would satisfy the address’s script in a transaction built around the message, so any address, whatever script controls it, can in principle be signed for. The signature comes in several formats, each new format marked by a three-letter prefix.

sections.heading: A verifier can also say “I cannot check this”

blocks.text: The verifier starts with the address, message and response. It reconstructs the virtual transactions, checks that they refer to each other correctly, and validates the script under BIP 322’s additional rules. In the explorer’s wrong-message example, the changed challenge makes the signature check fail.

The outcome is one of three states, not two. Invalid means some check failed. Inconclusive means the verifier could not check the scripts: a verifier without a full script interpreter should stop there for any script it does not understand, and the BIP’s upgradeable rules also end in inconclusive. Valid comes with two numbers, “valid at time T and age S”, where T is to_sign’s lock time and S is its first input’s sequence, so a signature that relies on a time lock says so.

blocks.title: Three verdicts
blocks.caption: One published vector for each state. The inconclusive one is a proof-of-funds signature: this site’s model does not decode proof-of-funds PSBTs, so it cannot check the scripts they satisfy.

blocks.text: A verifier that does not understand a script must not turn that gap into an assurance that the proof passed. This page’s verifier covers the published simple and full examples; proof-of-funds PSBTs and committed scripts outside its supported set remain inconclusive unless an earlier check has failed.

blocks.summary: Required verification rules and reported time locks

blocks.text: A verifier is given an address, a message and a signature. It computes to_spend from the message and address, decodes to_sign from the signature, checks that to_sign’s first input spends to_spend’s output and that it has exactly one output, and then checks that the pair satisfies the consensus rules, except that to_sign’s lock time and first sequence are not enforced but reported. (A simple signature has no to_sign to check; the verifier builds it.)

On top of consensus the BIP adds required rules. Every signature MUST use SIGHASH_ALL, or SIGHASH_DEFAULT where the output type supports it; CODESEPARATOR and FindAndDelete are forbidden; ECDSA signatures must be strictly DER-encoded with a low S value, and a failing one must be empty; pushes must be minimal; IF arguments must be exactly 0x01 or empty; and only a single stack element may remain. Breaking any of these makes the signature invalid.

This site’s model is such a partial verifier. Its script interpreter runs only a reviewed set of opcodes, enough for every published simple and full vector: P2PKH, P2SH, nested and native SegWit, multisig, Taproot key and script paths, and time locks. It applies the required rules in all of them, answers inconclusive for proof-of-funds signatures and for any committed script or spend shape outside what it covers, unless an earlier check has already failed, and rejects every published error vector. For a full signature, a wrong message or a wrong address fails before any script is run: it changes to_spend’s ID, so the transmitted to_sign no longer spends it. For a simple signature the verifier rebuilds to_sign around the new to_spend, and the signature no longer verifies.
